topic: The Building Blocks of Sound: Pure Fourier Sine Series

sections.title: The Mystery of the Square Wave
sections.content: Introduce a 'Musical Robot' named Oscillo who can only sing pure, smooth sine waves. Oscillo wants to mimic a harsh, blocky 'Square Wave' produced by a synthesizer. This sets the stage: how can smooth curves create sharp corners?
sections.example: Oscillo the Robot tries to match a jagged 1Hz square wave using only rounded 'S' shaped motions.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Symmetry and Periodicity
sections.content: Briefly review 'Odd Functions' (Symmetry around the origin). Explain that because a Square Wave is odd ($f(-x) = -f(x)$), we only need Pure Sine waves to describe it, skipping Cosines entirely. This simplifies our toolkit.
sections.example: An animation showing a sine wave being flipped across both the X and Y axes to show it perfectly overlaps with itself, just like our Square Wave target.

sections.title: The Harmonic Blueprint (The Formula)
sections.content: Present the Pure Sine Series formula: $f(x) = \sum b_n \sin(n\omega x)$. Explain that 'n' represents the harmonic number. Visualizing 'n=1' as the base note and 'n=3, 5, 7...' as the overtones.
sections.example: A graphic showing a guitar string vibrating as a whole (n=1), then in two halves (n=2), then three (n=3), each adding a higher pitch.

sections.title: The Projection Trick: Calculating Coefficients
sections.content: Explain $b_n$ using 'Graphical Overlap'. If we multiply our Square Wave by a specific Sine wave and the area under the resulting curve is large, that Sine wave is a 'strong ingredient'. This is the integral calculation visualized as a color-coded area.
sections.example: An animation showing a 1Hz Square wave multiplied by a 1Hz Sine wave (mostly positive area = large $b_1$) vs. a 1Hz Square wave multiplied by a 2Hz Sine wave (positive and negative areas cancel out = $b_2$ is zero).

sections.title: The Construction Site (Animation)
sections.content: A fast-paced visual assembly. Start with the fundamental sine wave. Layer by layer, add the 3rd, 5th, and 7th harmonics with decreasing amplitudes ($1/n$). Watch the 'wobbles' at the top of the wave flatten out into a straight line.
sections.example: As each sine wave is added, the 'corners' of the sum get sharper, showing how infinite smooth waves eventually create a perfect sharp corner.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Audio Compression
sections.content: Conclude with why this matters. Instead of storing every point of a complex sound wave, a computer only needs to store the 'recipe' (the $b_n$ values). This is the secret behind MP3s and digital communication.
sections.example: Oscillo the Robot sends a list of 5 numbers to a friend instead of a heavy recording; the friend uses the Fourier Series to 'rebuild' the sound perfectly.
